items.title: Vultrino – Let AI agents use credentials without seeing them
items.raw_excerpt:
I built Vultrino because I kept running into the same problem: I want AI agents to do things
that require credentials, but I don't want those secrets in prompts, logs, or context windows. It's not just API keys – it's signing commits with PGP keys, accessing databases, decrypting
files, anything that needs a secret. The agent shouldn't see the credential; it should just be
able to use it. Vultrino is a credential proxy that sits between your AI agent and the operation. The agent says "use my github-api credential" or "sign this with my pgp-key" and Vultrino handles the secret
material without exposing it. Key features:
- WASM plugin system – add any credential type (PGP signing plugin included, build your own)
- MCP native – works directly with Claude
- OAuth2 with automatic token refresh

- API tests (HTTP/GraphQL)
- Database tests (PostgreSQL, MySQL)
- k6 performance tests
- Schedule tests via cron or trigger from CI/CD Monitoring:
- HTTP, Website, Ping, Port monitors
- Synthetic mon

items.title: Don't Automate Chaos: The "100x Rule" of Factory AI
items.raw_excerpt: I spent years working at Sysmex (medical devices) and Toyota Group (automotive parts) in Japan. With the current AI boom, I see many companies trying to inject "Silicon Valley logic" (move fast and break things) into manufacturing floors. In my experience, this usually leads to what I call the "PoC Graveyard." In the physical world, bugs aren't just Jira tickets—they are injuries, recalls, or broken lines. I argue that before writing any code, we must follow the "100x Rule": Non-Standardized Process + AI = 100x Chaos Standardized Process + AI = 100x Profit If you automate a mess, you just get a faster mess. I put together my thoughts on why "Standardization" must strictly precede "Automation," along with a 5-step checklist I use to diagnose factory readiness.
